extracted.intended_audience: SDS and label preparers, chemical classifiers, manufacturers/importers, and hazard communication compliance personnel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for classifying and labeling chemicals that cause corrosion of the respiratory tract (including when to use STOT-SE, acute toxicity statements, pictograms, and how mixtures should be handled). Applies to preparation of labels and Safety Data Sheets (SDS) under the OSHA HCS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered approach for corrosive to the respiratory tract
rubrics_metrics.description: When classifying for corrosive to the respiratory tract the classifier should take a tiered approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If data indicate the chemical is corrosive to the respiratory tract and the effect leads to lethality, the label must contain the hazard statement “Corrosive to the respiratory tract” and the corrosion pictogram in addition to the prescribed acute toxicity hazard statement(s) and other label and SDS elements. If data indicate corrosive to the respiratory tract but does not lead to lethality, classify using STOT single exposure (STOT-SE) and include the hazard statement “Corrosive to the respiratory tract if inhaled.” This hazard statement should be used instead of a more general STOT-SE respiratory tract statement and the corrosion pictogram is required instead of the general health pictogram. If no direct respiratory data exist but the chemical is classified under skin corrosion/irritation or serious eye damage/irritation, the classifier must consider those data to determine whether the chemical may be corrosive to the respiratory tract and, if so, include the appropriate hazard statement and corrosion pictogram along with already-required statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of corrosion pictogram for respiratory corrosion under STOT
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is requiring the use of the more specific corrosion pictogram instead of the more general health pictogram when this hazard is addressed under STOT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When corrosive to the respiratory tract is addressed under STOT-SE, the corrosion pictogram must be used. However, if there are other target organ hazards, the current STOT hazard statement and pictogram should be used in addition to the required hazard statement and pictogram for corrosive to the respiratory tract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental hazard statement for lethal respiratory corrosivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If corrosivity to the respiratory tract leads to lethality, include the hazard statement “Corrosive to the respiratory tract” in addition to acute toxicity hazard statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA retains GHS wording for the supplemental hazard statement and disagrees that a modified, more explicit lethality wording (e.g., 'can cause death if inhaled') is required because acute toxicity statements already convey lethality (e.g., 'Fatal if inhaled').

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrosive to the respiratory tract is not a distinct hazard class
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'corrosive to the respiratory tract' hazard is not a distinct hazard class and therefore no hazard categories or cut-off values will be established specifically for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification of mixtures follows the same principles as for other health hazards; corrosive respiratory effects are communicated via existing hazard classes (acute toxicity, STOT-SE, skin corrosion/irritation, or eye damage/irritation) and the associated pictograms, signal words, hazard statements and precautionary statements, plus the added 'Corrosive to the respiratory tract' or 'Corrosive to the respiratory tract, if inhaled' language as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate STOT categories for respiratory corrosion
rubrics_metrics.description: STOT-SE Category 1 and Category 2 are appropriate for classifying corrosive to the respiratory tract when data indicate non-lethality; STOT-RE is not appropriate; STOT-SE Category 3 is not appropriate for respiratory corrosion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA maintains that STOT-SE (A.8) Category 1 and 2 criteria can cover local effects and that STOT-RE (A.9) should be excluded for this hazard because respiratory tract corrosion is an acute effect. OSHA removed the reference to STOT-RE from A.1.2.4.2 and did not include a note for STOT-SE Category 3 in Appendix C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture classification and communication when components are corrosive to respiratory tract
rubrics_metrics.description: If mixtures contain components deemed corrosive to the respiratory tract, classify and label the mixture according to the applicable hazard class and include the respiratory corrosion statement on the SDS and label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no data are available for the mixture as a whole, classify the mixture based on component data as acutely toxic, STOT-SE, skin corrosion/irritation, or eye damage/irritation and carry the appropriate pictogram(s), signal word, hazard statement(s) and precautionary statement(s). The SDS and label for the mixture will also contain 'Corrosive to the respiratory tract' (for acute toxicity, skin corrosion/irritation, or eye damage/irritation) or 'Corrosive to the respiratory tract, if inhaled' (for STOT-SE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Label element consolidation and flexibilities (Appendix C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple hazards require the same pictogram only one pictogram should appear on the label; label preparers have flexibilities to omit or modify statements to improve readability and may add supplemental information so long as it does not contradict required information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Appendix C: C.3.2.4 (one pictogram if multiple hazards require the same pictogram), C.2 (Hazard statements) and C.4 (Precautionary statements) for flexibilities to omit or modify statements when inappropriate or to improve readability. Label preparers can provide supplemental information to the label or SDS provided it does not contradict or cast doubt on required information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unknown acute toxicity statement for mixtures (A.1.3.6.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require a statement on the label and SDS that 'X percent of the mixture consists of ingredient(s) of unknown acute (oral/dermal/inhalation) toxicity' where applicable, differentiated by route of exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statement is required where the mixture is already classified as acutely toxic for a particular route and there are one or more relevant ingredients of unknown acute toxicity for that route present at ≥1%. If the mixture as a whole has been tested but not classified, no statement is required. If the mixture has not been tested as a whole, classify based on known ingredients and include the statement where appropriate. OSHA will update Hazard Classification guidance with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: ATE formula units and guidance (A.1.3.6.1 / Table A.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Table A.1.1 provides the units that should be used to calculate the Acute Toxicity Estimate (ATE) by route of exposure; the ATE formula was not changed in the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's Hazard Classification guidance document provides guidance and examples using the ATE formula (Document ID 0008, pp. 33-35). Comments requesting additional unit examples were noted but the formula remains as proposed; Table A.1.1 lists applicable units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split entry concept not supported under HCS
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCS classification process does not support the use of the 'split entry' concept for modifying GHS classification based on differences (e.g., particle size) between test samples and supplied form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's 2013 LOI describes split entry and explains it is not supported under HCS 2012; OSHA will consider addressing this issue in updated guidance but currently the use of 'split entry' is not allowed under the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of Rev. 8 changes to skin corrosion/irritation (Appendix A.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA aligns Appendix A.2 with Rev. 8 updates to Chapter 3.2 including a tiered evaluation approach and expanded use of non-animal test methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Updates include recognition of specific in vitro test methods, reorganization of the tiered approach with a new decision logic diagram (Figure 3.2.1/Table A.2.1), elevation of in vitro data acceptance to tier 2, and consideration of conflicting lower-tiered data when a lower tier suggests a higher classification. OSHA retains that all available and relevant information must be considered and that classifications must be based on data generated using internationally validated and accepted methods. Inclusion of Rev. 8 updates does not require re-evaluation of already-classified chemicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Updated definitions and time parameters for skin corrosion and irritation (A.2.1.1 / A.2.2.x)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised definitions clarify 'initial' exposure and time parameters: 'Skin corrosion refers to the production of irreversible damage to the skin; namely, visible necrosis through the epidermis and into the dermis occurring after initial exposure...' and 'Skin irritation refers to the production of reversible damage to the skin occurring after initial exposure...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA added 'initial' to definitions and included time parameters in classification text: for skin irritation language such as 'following its application for up to 4 hours' (consistent with OECD test guidelines) is retained; paragraphs A.2.2.2.1.1 and A.2.2.2.2.1/2 clarify when 'initial' and 'following first application' apply to Category 1/2 decisions. OSHA kept the GHS/OECD phrasing for consistency and classifier familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence of data evaluation and tiered evaluation approach for skin corrosion/irritation
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifiers must consider all available and relevant information when conducting classifications and follow a tiered evaluation approach (per Rev. 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraphs based on Rev. 8 clarify that all classifications must be based on data generated using internationally validated and accepted methods and that the tiered approach (as presented in Figure A.2.1/Table A.2.1) guides the sequence of evidence (including in vitro, read-across, SAR, and in vivo data) for determining skin corrosion/irritation categories.
